title: I. The Beginning Of Perhotin’s Official Career
paragraphs: Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, whom we left knocking at the stoutly locked gates of the widow Morozov's house, ended, naturally enough, by making himself heard. Fenya, still shaken from the fright she'd had two hours earlier and too "upset" to go to bed, was nearly startled into hysterics by the furious knocking at the gate. Though she'd watched Mitya drive off herself, she imagined it must be Dmitri Fyodorovitch knocking again — no one else could knock so savagely. She ran to the house porter, who'd already woken and gone out to the gate, and begged him not to open it. But after questioning Pyotr Ilyitch and learning that he wanted to see Fenya on very "important business," the man finally decided to let him in. Pyotr Ilyitch was shown into Fenya's kitchen, though the girl asked him to let the porter stay, "on account of her misgivings." He began questioning her and immediately learned the crucial fact: that when Dmitri Fyodorovitch had run out to look for Grushenka, he'd snatched up a pestle from the mortar, and that when he came back, the pestle wasn't with him, and his hands were smeared with blood.

"And the blood was just flowing off him, dripping, dripping!" Fenya kept exclaiming. This horrifying detail was purely the product of her overwrought imagination. But though it hadn't been "dripping," Pyotr Ilyitch had seen the blood-stained hands himself, and had even helped wash them. Besides, the question he had to settle wasn't how quickly the blood had dried, but where Dmitri Fyodorovitch had run off to with the pestle — or rather, whether it really had been to Fyodor Pavlovitch's, and how he might confirm it for certain. Pyotr Ilyitch kept circling back to this point, and though he turned up nothing conclusive, he came away convinced that Dmitri Fyodorovitch could have gone nowhere else but his father's house, and that something must have happened there.

"And when he came back," Fenya added, agitated, "I told him the whole story, and then I started asking him, 'Why is there blood on your hands, Dmitri Fyodorovitch?' and he told me it was human blood, and that he'd just killed someone. He confessed it all to me, and then suddenly ran off like a madman. I sat down and started thinking — where's he run off to now, like a madman? He'll go to Mokroe, I thought, and kill my mistress there. I ran out to beg him not to kill her. I was running toward his lodgings, but I glanced at Plotnikov's shop and saw him just setting off, and there was no blood on his hands then." (Fenya had noticed this, and remembered it.) Fenya's old grandmother backed up her account as far as she was able. After a few more questions, Pyotr Ilyitch left the house even more unsettled and uneasy than when he'd arrived.

The most direct and simplest thing for him to do would have been to go straight to Fyodor Pavlovitch's, to find out whether anything had happened there, and if so, what — and only go to the police captain, as Pyotr Ilyitch firmly intended to, once he'd confirmed the facts. But the night was dark, Fyodor Pavlovitch's gates were sturdy, and he'd have to knock again. He barely knew Fyodor Pavlovitch, and what if, after all that knocking, they let him in and nothing had happened at all? Then Fyodor Pavlovitch, in his mocking way, would tell the story all over town — how some stranger named Perhotin had burst in on him at midnight to ask whether anyone had killed him. It would make a scandal. And scandal was what Pyotr Ilyitch dreaded more than anything in the world.

And yet the feeling gripping him was so strong that, though he stamped his foot angrily and cursed himself, he set off again — not to Fyodor Pavlovitch's, but to Madame Hohlakov's. He decided that if she denied having just given Dmitri Fyodorovitch three thousand roubles, he'd go straight to the police captain; but if she admitted giving him the money, he'd go home and let the matter rest until morning.

It's plain enough, of course, that going to a fashionable lady, a complete stranger, at eleven at night, and perhaps rousing her from bed to ask her a startling question, was even more likely to cause a scandal than going to Fyodor Pavlovitch. But that's just how it goes, sometimes, especially in cases like this one, with even the most precise and even-tempered people's decisions. Pyotr Ilyitch was anything but even-tempered at that moment. He remembered all his life how a haunting unease had gradually taken hold of him, growing more and more painful, driving him on against his own will. Yet, of course, he kept cursing himself the whole way for going to this lady, but "I'll get to the bottom of it, I will!" he repeated for the tenth time, grinding his teeth, and carried out his plan.

It was exactly eleven o'clock when he entered Madame Hohlakov's house. He was let into the yard readily enough, but when he asked whether the lady was still up, the porter had no answer to give him, beyond saying she was usually in bed by that hour.
"Ask upstairs. If the lady wants to see you, she'll see you. If she won't, she won't."

Pyotr Ilyitch went up, but found things not so simple here. The footman was reluctant to take in his name, but finally called for a maid. Pyotr Ilyitch, politely but insistently, asked her to tell her mistress that an official living in town, named Perhotin, had come on particular business, and that if it weren't of the greatest importance he wouldn't have dared to come. "Tell her exactly that, word for word," he asked the girl.

She went off. He waited in the entry. Madame Hohlakov herself was already in her bedroom, though not yet asleep. She'd been unsettled ever since Mitya's visit, and had a feeling she wouldn't get through the night without the sick headache that always followed such upsets, for her. She was startled to hear the maid's announcement. She irritably refused to see him at first, though the unexpected visit at such an hour, from an "official living in town" who was a total stranger, sharply piqued her feminine curiosity. But this time Pyotr Ilyitch was as stubborn as a mule. He earnestly begged the maid to carry another message back, in these exact words:
"That he had come on business of the greatest importance, and that Madame Hohlakov might have cause to regret it later, if she refused to see him now."
"I threw myself in headlong," he described it afterward.

The maid, staring at him in astonishment, went to deliver the message again. Madame Hohlakov was impressed. She thought it over a moment, asked what he looked like, and learned that he was "very well dressed, young, and so polite." We might note, in passing, that Pyotr Ilyitch was a rather good-looking young man, and well aware of it. Madame Hohlakov made up her mind to see him. She was in her dressing gown and slippers, but she threw a black shawl over her shoulders. "The official" was shown into the drawing room — the very same room Mitya had been received in shortly before. The lady came to meet her visitor with a sternly questioning look, and, without asking him to sit, began at once:
"What do you want?"
"I've taken the liberty of disturbing you, madam, on a matter concerning our mutual acquaintance, Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov," Perhotin began.
But he'd barely gotten the name out when the lady's face showed signs of intense irritation. She very nearly shrieked, cutting him off in a fury:

"How much longer am I to be tormented by that dreadful man?" she cried, hysterically. "How dare you, sir, how could you possibly presume to disturb a lady who is a complete stranger to you, in her own home, at such an hour!... And to force yourself on her to talk about a man who came here, to this very drawing room, only three hours ago, to murder me, and stormed out of the room the way no one would leave a decent house. Let me tell you, sir, I intend to lodge a complaint against you, I won't let this pass. Kindly leave at once.... I am a mother.... I ... I—"
"Murder! Then he tried to murder you too?"
"Why, has he killed someone else?" Madame Hohlakov asked, impulsively.

"If you'll kindly listen for half a moment, madam, I'll explain everything in a couple of words," Perhotin answered, firmly. "At five o'clock this afternoon Dmitri Fyodorovitch borrowed ten roubles from me, and I know for a fact he had no money. Yet at nine o'clock he came to see me with a bundle of hundred-rouble notes in his hand — some two or three thousand roubles. His hands and face were covered in blood, and he looked like a madman. When I asked where he'd gotten so much money, he told me he'd just received it from you, that you'd given him three thousand to go to the gold mines...."
Madame Hohlakov's face took on an expression of intense, agonized excitement.

"Good God! He must have killed his own father!" she cried, clasping her hands. "I never gave him money, never! Oh, go, run!... Don't say another word! Save the old man ... run to his father's ... run!"
"Excuse me, madam — so you didn't give him money? You're certain, as a matter of fact, that you gave him nothing?"

"No, I didn't, I didn't! I refused to give it to him, because he couldn't appreciate it. He ran out furious, stamping his feet. He lunged at me, but I slipped away.... And let me tell you, since I mean to hide nothing from you now, that he actually spat at me. Can you imagine! But why are we standing here? Ah, do sit down."
"Excuse me, I...."
"Or better yet, run, run, you must run and save that poor old man from a horrible death!"
"But what if he's already killed him?"
"Ah, good heavens, yes! Then what are we to do now? What do you think we should do?"

Meanwhile she'd gotten Pyotr Ilyitch to sit, and sat down herself, facing him. Briefly but fairly clearly, Pyotr Ilyitch told her the whole story — at least the part of it he'd witnessed himself. He described, too, his visit to Fenya, and told her about the pestle. All these details produced an overwhelming effect on the distraught lady, who kept letting out shrieks and covering her face with her hands....

"Would you believe it, I foresaw all of this! I have that particular gift — whatever I imagine comes to pass. And how many times have I looked at that dreadful man and thought, that man will end up murdering me. And now it's happened ... that is, if he hasn't murdered me, only his own father, it's only because the finger of God preserved me, and what's more, he was ashamed to murder me, because right here, in this very spot, I placed the holy icon holding relics of the holy martyr Saint Varvara around his neck.... And to think how close I came to death at that instant, I walked right up to him and he stretched his neck out to me!... Do you know, Pyotr Ilyitch — I believe you said your name was Pyotr Ilyitch — I don't believe in miracles, but that icon, and this unmistakable miracle just now, that shakes me, I'm ready to believe anything you like. Have you heard of Father Zossima?... But I don't know what I'm saying ... and just imagine, with the icon around his neck he spat at me.... He only spat, it's true, he didn't murder me, and ... he dashed off! But what are we to do, what must we do now? What do you think?"
Pyotr Ilyitch got up and announced that he was going straight to the police captain, to tell him everything and leave him to decide what to do.

"Oh, he's an excellent man, excellent! Mihail Makarovitch, I know him. Of course, he's the man to go to. How practical you are, Pyotr Ilyitch! How well you've thought this all through! I'd never have thought of it, in your place!"

"Especially since I know the police captain quite well myself," Pyotr Ilyitch observed, still standing, visibly anxious to get away from this impulsive lady as quickly as possible — she wouldn't even let him say goodbye and leave.

"And mind, mind," she prattled on, "come back and tell me what you find there, what you learn ... what comes out ... how they'll try him ... what he's sentenced to.... Tell me, we don't have capital punishment, do we? But be sure to come, even if it's three in the morning, or four, or half past four.... Tell them to wake me, to shake me awake if I'm not up.... But, good heavens, I shan't sleep a wink! But wait — hadn't I better come with you?"
"N—no. But if you'd write three lines in your own hand, stating that you didn't give Dmitri Fyodorovitch any money, it might be useful ... in case it's needed...."

"Of course!" Madame Hohlakov skipped over to her writing desk, delighted. "And you know, I'm simply astonished, amazed, at your resourcefulness, your good sense in matters like this. Are you in government service here? I'm delighted to think you're in service here!"
And still talking, she scribbled the following lines on half a sheet of notepaper:

I have never in my life lent that unhappy man, Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov (for, whatever else, he is unhappy), three thousand roubles, today or any day. I have never given him money, never: this I swear by all that is holy!
K. HOHLAKOV.
"Here's the note!" she turned quickly to Pyotr Ilyitch. "Go, save him. It's a noble thing you're doing!"
And she made the sign of the cross over him three times. She ran out to see him off to the passage.

"How grateful I am to you! You can't imagine how grateful I am that you came to me first. How is it we've never met before? I shall be flattered to see you at my house from now on. How delightful that you live here!... Such precision! Such practical ability!... People ought to appreciate you, they ought to understand you. If there's ever anything I can do, believe me ... oh, I love young people! I'm in love with young people! The younger generation is the one support of our suffering country. Her one hope.... Oh, go, go!..."

But Pyotr Ilyitch had already fled — or she'd never have let him go so soon. Still, Madame Hohlakov had left him a rather pleasant impression, one that softened somewhat his uneasiness at being dragged into such an unpleasant affair. Tastes differ, as we all know. "She's really not so old," he thought, pleased, "quite the opposite, I'd have taken her for her own daughter."

As for Madame Hohlakov, she was simply enchanted by the young man. "Such sense! Such precision! In so young a man! In this day and age! And with such manners, such looks besides! People say the young people of today are good for nothing, but here's living proof otherwise!" and so on. So she simply forgot the whole "dreadful affair," and it was only as she was climbing into bed, suddenly recalling "how close to death she'd come," that she exclaimed: "Ah, it's awful, awful!"
But she dropped at once into a sound, sweet sleep.

I wouldn't, however, have lingered over such trivial and beside-the-point details, if this odd meeting between the young official and the not-at-all-elderly widow hadn't later turned out to lay the foundation for that practical, precise young man's entire career. His story is still remembered with astonishment in our town to this day, and I may perhaps have something to say about it once I've finished this long history of the Brothers Karamazov.
